summary: Clarify soft-reject window and rate-slice behavior for mixed SSE long-lived sessions + bulk webhook backfills
description: Issue summary: Customer Streamlytics reports a recurring pattern of 'soft' 429 rejections during large daily webhook backfills while maintaining dozens of long-lived SSE streams to our API. They see intermittent 429s that do not align with console quota depletion and disagree with expected per-route vs per-tenant accounting. Impact: Production ingestion pipelines and real-time dashboards show spikes in failed webhook callbacks (5-8% of batch jobs) between 02:00-03:30 UTC during the nightly backfill window, and low-latency SSE consumers intermittently receive 'connection rejected' events. Customer requests clarification on how the soft-reject/grace window and rate-slicing work for long-lived connections + bulk background jobs, and asks for immediate mitigation guidance.
steps_to_reproduce:
1) Maintain 40 active SSE connections from a single API key (keepalive every 30s) for realtime updates.
2) Trigger a backfill job that makes 12k webhook POSTs over 20 minutes using the same API key but via a separate route (/hooks/bulk).
3) Monitor client logs and the API response headers for 429, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, and Retry-After.
4) Observe a wave of 'soft' 429s starting ~5 minutes into the backfill that persist for ~10-15 minutes, then taper.
5) Console shows remaining credits non-zero and not fully exhausted at start of the wave.
observed_behavior:
- Intermittent 429 responses with Retry-After present (seconds vary).
- Console shows burst credits still available for the tenant.
- Sample response header from customer capture: 'X-RateLimit-Limit: 60000; X-RateLimit-Remaining: 4321; Retry-After: 8'
- SSE connections report reconnection attempts and occasional 'reject' events but most streams recover automatically.
- Backfill job logs show retries cause significant backoff and extend the window beyond maintenance window causing missed SLAs.
expected_behavior:
- Background bulk backfills should consume from a separate burst pool or be rate-sliced so long-lived low-throughput SSE sessions are not affected.
- When console shows available tenant burst credits, customer should not observe sustained 429 waves across routes unless refill window misalignment or health probes are double-counting credits.

investigation_notes:
Initial hypotheses: 1) Backfill requests and SSE keepalives are counted against the same tenant bucket; synchronous fanout plus retries cause short-term token depletion and early rejects despite console showing non-zero bucket due to epoched refill behavior. 2) Health checks or probe traffic from the customer's orchestrator may be counted double due to path normalization between edge and origin. 3) Priority lane borrowing/weighting: background route (/hooks/bulk) might be configured at same priority as SSE route; smoothing and grace windows can cause background jobs to dip into low-latency lanes during scale-up.
What we checked: - Reviewed rate-limiter epochs for tenant id t-7821; saw refill epochs at 02:00 and 02:05 UTC with a staggered window on edge vs origin leading to short drift. - Correlated proxy logs: repeated preflight (OPTIONS) from customer orchestrator seen at ~02:06 counted separately on the edge. - Check of dedicated-pool config: customer is enterprise on shared hosted capacity (not dedicated); no isolated burst pool is provisioned. - Looked at recent config changes: no global rate window changes in last 30 days.
Partial findings: - Refill window drift (edge vs origin) can produce a temporary mis-read in console: credits shown are after origin refill but edge counters still enforce pre-refill state, causing 'soft' rejects during the drift window. - Retries amplify the sawtooth and create a self-reinforcing wave.
Next steps: - Reproduce in sandbox with controlled SSE + bulk job (assigned to Lucas). - Propose immediate mitigation: ask customer to reduce concurrency of backfill to 150 RPS and add jittered exponential backoff to retries; advise temporary split of API keys per route to isolate burst budgets. - Longer term: Ops/RateLimiter team to evaluate providing an 'exempted long-lived session' pool or route-based burst isolation for enterprise customers.
comments: Aisha Khan (support): Collected request traces and initial symptom report from customer. They are hitting this nightly and it's causing missed SLAs for dashboards. Customer asks for both immediate mitigation and architecture guidance to avoid reoccurrence.

Lucas Meyer (SRE): Assigned to reproduce in sandbox with 40 SSE sims + 12k POSTs. I see refill epoch skew between edge and origin; replicating scheduled backfill reproduces the 10-15m soft 429 wave. Will attach sandbox runbook once complete.

SRE (note): Confirmed preflight OPTIONS from orchestrator were being counted separately due to path normalization. Added a filter rule suggestion to ignore internal health-check user-agent patterns during rate accounting for this tenant.

Customer (Streamlytics - Maya R.): We will try splitting API keys per route and throttle our backfill to 150 RPS in the short term. Can you confirm whether long-lived SSEs can be exempted from burst accounting?
resolution_notes:
Workarounds provided: 1) Short-term: create two API keys (one for SSE long-lived connections, one for bulk backfills). This isolates burst accounting and eliminated cross-interference in customer's staging tests. 2) Throttle recommendation: limit backfill concurrency to <=150 RPS from single host, add 100-300ms jitter to retry loops. 3) Console guidance: customer to monitor X-RateLimit-Remaining and defer aggressive retrying when Retry-After present.
Engineering action items: - RateLimiter team to evaluate a 'long-lived session exemption' feature and a route-based burst pool for enterprise tenants (ticketed as INT-2102). - Ops to patch edge-origin epoch alignment to reduce refill drift (PR referenced).
Follow-up: Customer confirmed reduced failures in staging after applying isolate-key approach and throttling. We scheduled a technical review with them for 2026-03-18 to discuss dedicated burst pools for their workload.
Status: Mitigated (customer-level workaround applied); engineering follow-up required.
